topic: Procoder: Senior-Developer Commit Gate Discipline for Coding Agents

key_points: One dependency-free Go binary gives coding agents a commit gate (procoder check) they cannot talk their way past
Gate counts 'unchecked' as failing — a tool that could not run is never reported as clean
Covers formatting across 15+ languages, git hygiene (conflict markers, junk, oversized files, AI-attribution), secrets, lint, CI/infra, docs — one code path so check/git/CI never disagree
Two modes: self-serve tools the agent runs + forced hooks (every write, every session start) it cannot skip
P-CONTROL principle: binary computes, agent reasons, agent changes — nothing edits code behind the agent's back
Works with 20+ agents (Claude Code, Cursor, Windsurf, Cline, Kilo Code, Roo, Kiro, Codex CLI, Copilot CLI, Gemini, OpenCode, AGENTS.md readers)
Quick start for Claude Code: /plugin marketplace add azrtydxb/procoder; /plugin install procoder; /procoder:init
Divio-documented site: tutorial, how-to, reference, explanation
Quality chain: spec interview, plan, backlog (milestones→epics→user stories), scope-boxed sprints, acceptance-criteria TODOs, pre-PR self-review, release control
Core differentiator is 'refusal, not advice' — todo close refuses without evidence, sprint close refuses to hide unfinished work, release lists every reason the tag is not earned
Ten check domains: security, lint, maintainability/dependency freshness, performance/benchmarks, documentation/ADRs, formatting, testing, CI, infra, GitOps
Self-learning loop: every escaped bug records a lesson and requires a permanent adaptation (lint rule, regression test, rubric entry) to close the bug's whole class
Procoder consolidates three earlier community tools (Superpowers, Ponytail, Serena) into one binary
Rule is simple: agent can't mark work done if verification is incomplete; escaped bugs require a permanent fix (new lint rule or pinned test) before close
Growing steadily ~21 stars/day rather than viral burst — signals broad realization that agents shouldn't certify their own work
Businesses putting coding agents in production need checks that verify evidence and make recurring mistakes less likely
Frames the problem: agents can produce work, but they shouldn't be trusted to certify their own work (self-certification flaw)
Four mandatory quality gates for AI-generated commits: Style & Correctness → Security Scan → Test Coverage → Compliance Verify, ordered by cost
Zero-tolerance config for agents — agents can't earn warning suppressions the way humans can; human-authored override commit required
Cites Stanford (Perry et al. 2023): AI-assistant users write less secure code AND over-rate their own insecure output
Key idea: 'stop trusting appearances and start trusting evidence' — gates convert human-review burden into deterministic CI evidence
AI code can pass a test yet still hide drift, scope creep, brittle fixes
Three-layer pre-commit verification: versioned inputs lock the conditions of generation, deterministic validation nodes test boundaries/policy, human-readable report for traceability
Separates generation stage from validation stage (deterministic agentic nodes)
LLM agents are probabilistic — same input doesn't guarantee same output, so deterministic gates matter

stats.fact: In Veracode's 2025 GenAI Code Security Report, 45% of code samples generated by 100+ LLMs failed security tests and introduced OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities.
Java was the riskiest AI-generated language at 72% security failure rate; Python 38%, JavaScript 43%, C# 45% in the same Veracode study.
AI tools failed to defend against Cross-Site Scripting (CWE-80) in 86% of relevant code samples (Veracode 2025).
GitClear's analysis of 623M changes (2023-2026) found refactoring down 70%, code block duplication up 81%, and error-masking up 47% as AI authorship scales.
GitClear: copy/pasted code rose from 8% to ~12-18% of changes while refactored/moved code fell from 25% (2021) to under 10% (2024-2025) across 211M+ lines.
Cloned/duplicated code is independently linked to 15-50% more defects (GitClear).
Stanford (Perry et al., 2023): developers using AI assistants wrote significantly LESS secure code and rated their own insecure output as more secure.
Demirer, Musolff & Yang (May 2026): autonomous coding agents increased commits by ~180%, but the effect fell to 50% for projects started and 30% for actual releases.
Procoder (github.com/azrtydxb/procoder) is a single Go binary with no runtime dependencies, Apache 2.0 licensed, supporting 20+ coding agents (created 2026-08-16).
Procoder was growing steadily at ~21 stars/day as of late August 2026 (~139 stars), signaling steady organic adoption rather than a viral spike (Enterprise DNA).

angles: Self-certification trap: agents shouldn't be trusted to certify their own work — 'done' must survive an external gate, not just what the agent says
Refusal over advice: the difference between skills/instructions that an agent can ignore vs deterministic gates that refuse to progress on FAIL or UNCHECKED
Unchecked counts as failing: the single most important design principle — a tool that couldn't run is never 'clean', closing the honesty gap
Concrete setup path for a real repo: install, init, run procoder check, watch it block, fix, pass — a senior-dev discipline walkthrough
The lessons loop: closing a bug's whole class with a permanent lint rule/regression test, not just fixing the symptom
Agent-agnostic portability: one .procoder/ config + AGENTS.md works across Claude Code, Cursor, Codex, Copilot, etc.
Forced vs self-serve: why hooks at write/session boundaries matter more than polite instructions for autonomous agents
keywords: verify AI agent code before commit
enforce engineering discipline on AI agents
